channel.title: California Uzbek — Latest
channel.description: Independent analysis · Central Asia & world geopolitics

item.title: Germany's Deutsche Bahn offers Uzbek construction workers jobs starting at €3,418 a month
item.description: Germany's national rail operator is recruiting construction specialists through Uzbekistan's Migration Agency: a starting gross salary of €3,418, 30 days of paid leave and free German-language training in Tashkent.

item.title: One in three Germans backs anti-Muslim statements, Leipzig study finds
item.description: The University of Leipzig's 2026 Authoritarianism Study: anti-Muslim attitudes reach 34.1%, right-wing extremism has doubled, and satisfaction with democracy is at the lowest level in the survey's history.

item.title: Israel detains foreign activists who helped Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank
item.description: Israeli forces detained international volunteers aiding the olive harvest in the occupied West Bank and ordered a group deported; the Israeli group Yesh Din recorded 672 settler attacks in five weeks.

item.title: Forced labour persists in Turkmenistan's cotton harvest
item.description: Teachers, doctors and state employees are forced to pick cotton or to pay from their salaries for a replacement; reform pledges are not being met.

item.title: Uzbekistan joins the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO), 1992
item.description: On 28 November 1992 Uzbekistan, together with six other newly independent states, joined the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) founded by Iran, Pakistan and Turkey. The step opened sea-access routes and regional trade corridors for the young state — the organization's history, aims and significance for Uzbekistan, facts only.

item.title: Halal investing: how stocks are screened for Shari'ah compliance
item.description: Why buying a share differs from a bond, how shares are vetted through a two-step Shari'ah screen (business activity and financial ratios), how the AAOIFI, Dow Jones Islamic Market and MSCI standards differ, and what dividend "purification" (tat-hir) means — a facts-only explainer.

item.title: Trump: Israel and Gulf allies should repay the cost of the Iran war
item.description: In a CBS '60 Minutes' interview the US president said the countries it protects should repay the cost of the 2026 Iran war; analysts called it political rhetoric.

item.title: The second hijra of Uzbek émigrés from Afghanistan (1979–1992): a "doubly displaced" community
item.description: The descendants of Turkestani émigrés who fled Soviet rule into northern Afghanistan in the 1920s–30s were forced to flee again from the 1979 Soviet invasion — to Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey. The history of an Uzbek community that became refugees twice within a few generations, facts only.

item.title: Uzbekistan's annual inflation reached 6.5% in October
item.description: According to the Statistics Committee, prices rose 0.6% over the month; fuel, propane, meat and transport rose sharply.

item.title: Russia, Ukraine and the US begin talks in Abu Dhabi
item.description: The first trilateral meeting since February; the two-day session focused on future security guarantees.

item.title: How news media make money, and how bias arises
item.description: "Follow the money": advertising, subscriptions, membership, state funding and syndication — the revenue sources of media outlets and how each creates a slant (bias) in story selection, explained facts-only. A media-literacy explainer.

item.title: 67% of Uzbekistan's media is now privately owned, says Sherzod Asadov
item.description: At the third Uzbekistan–Russia Media Forum in Tashkent, the presidential press secretary said 67% of the country's media is private; internet coverage has reached 94%.

item.title: Uzbekistan to launch '1,000 Engineer-Designers' programme in 2027
item.description: According to the Presidential Press Service, local specialists will be sent to South Korea, Japan, China, Türkiye and European countries for advanced training.

item.title: The Volga (Kazan) Tatars in Uzbekistan: how a merchant and educator community took shape
item.description: The Volga (Kazan) Tatars are part of Uzbekistan's centuries-old multi-ethnic society. They came to Turkestan mainly in the 19th century, under Tsarist Russia, as merchants, interpreters, teachers and mullahs, acting as trade and cultural intermediaries. Their numbers grew in the Soviet era, including through the 1941–1945 wartime evacuation: the 1979 census recorded 531,205 Tatars, and the 1989 census 467,829 (2.4% of the population). After independence many emigrated to Russia, and by 2017 the number had fallen to about 195,000. This is a community distinct from the Crimean Tatars, a separate people deported here in 1944. History — facts only.

item.title: The U.S. court system and jury duty: the basics for immigrants
item.description: The U.S. has two parallel court systems: the federal courts (94 district courts → 13 courts of appeals → the Supreme Court) and each of the 50 states' own courts. A criminal case is brought by the government; a civil case is usually a private dispute. The Constitution guarantees the right to a jury. To serve on a federal jury you must be a U.S. CITIZEN: green-card or visa holders cannot serve. If you are summoned by mistake, do not ignore it — fill out the form and indicate you are not a citizen. A reference — facts only, not legal advice.

item.title: Uzbekistan finds advertising violations by 12 of 110 monitored bloggers
item.description: The Competition Committee monitors 110 bloggers' social media pages daily; 12 faced administrative liability, and scrutiny is expanding to well-known singers, actors and athletes.

item.title: Trump admits his deportation policy 'might have been too tough'
item.description: In a CBS '60 Minutes' interview Donald Trump said he is open to an immigration deal with Democrats; the same day he named Stephen Miller White House chief of staff.

item.title: How investing in gold works: forms, pricing, the halal rules and zakat
item.description: Gold is a familiar store of savings for many families. There are several ways to own it: physical bars and coins, jewellery, an allocated or unallocated bank account, a gold ETF, mining stocks and futures. The gold price is set on the international spot market, quoted per troy ounce (31.1035 grams) in US dollars. Gold pays no income (no interest or dividend) and its price can fall. In Islam gold is a "ribawi" commodity: it must be traded spot, hand-to-hand. The zakat nisab for gold is 85 grams of pure gold, at a rate of 2.5%. A reference — facts only, not financial advice.

item.title: Two disasters in one day: at least 21 die off Crete, 39 off Senegal
item.description: At least 21 migrants died off southern Crete, Greece, while at least 39 died when a boat bound for Spain's Canary Islands sank off Senegal.

item.title: Uzbekistan and UNESCO: membership and the World Heritage sites, a history (1993–2026)
item.description: Independent Uzbekistan became a member of UNESCO in 1993 and that same year, on 13 January, acceded to the 1972 World Heritage Convention by succession. Today the country has 8 sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List (6 cultural, 2 natural): Itchan Kala in Khiva (1990), the Historic Centre of Bukhara (1993), the Historic Centre of Shakhrisyabz (2000), Samarkand (2001), Western Tien-Shan (2016), the Cold Winter Deserts of Turan (2023), the Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor (2023) and Tashkent Modernist Architecture (2026). Shakhrisyabz has been on the "heritage in danger" list since 2016. History — facts only.

item.title: Qatar's PM to meet Trump: US rejects Iran's 'two-day' proposal
item.description: Iran, through Qatari mediation, put forward a phased plan; Washington rejected it, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling the terms 'outrageous and ridiculous.'

item.title: Bukharan students sent to Germany (1922): the Jadids' dream of knowledge, and the purge
item.description: In 1922 the government of the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic sent a group of young people to Germany for higher education. In all, about 70 students from Bukhara and Turkestan were sent to Germany; roughly 56 of them were from Bukhara, and 44 were placed in Berlin schools that summer. The initiative is linked mainly to the education minister (later prime minister) Abdurauf Fitrat. After the republic was abolished in 1924 the students were recalled; in the 1930s purges many were shot or exiled as "nationalists" or under "foreign influence," while some remained abroad as émigrés. History — documented facts only.

item.title: Kyrgyzstan issues housing documents to 295 households in Qorayantoq, a village transferred from Uzbekistan
item.description: The village was transferred from the Fergana region to the Batken region in 2024; a water network, a school and a kindergarten are now being built there.

item.title: The TRACECA transport corridor (1993–1998): independent Uzbekistan's search for routes to the world
item.description: TRACECA — the "Transport Corridor Europe–Caucasus–Asia" — is a programme launched by the European Union at a conference in Brussels in May 1993, aimed at developing a route connecting Central Asia to Europe across the Caspian, the Caucasus and the Black Sea, bypassing Russian territory. Uzbekistan was one of the programme's eight founding states. On 8 September 1998 the Basic Multilateral Agreement (MLA) was signed in Baku; 12 states adopted the document and a permanent secretariat was based in Baku. In the first years of independence this was part of Uzbekistan's policy of diversifying its transport routes. History — facts only.

item.title: Qard hasan: how a benevolent, interest-free loan works in Islam
item.description: Qard hasan — Arabic for "a beautiful loan" — is an interest-free, benevolent loan given to someone in need in Islam. The borrower repays only the principal received; no interest or markup is taken, because that would be riba. The Qur'an mentions the concept in several verses (for example al-Baqara 2:245, al-Hadid 57:11, al-Taghabun 64:17). Qard hasan differs from charity: charity is not repaid, but a loan is. A reference — facts only.

item.title: Energy Ministry: methane filling stations may be temporarily restricted during cold days
item.description: Temperatures drop sharply on 9–12 November; natural gas is directed first to homes and social facilities, with methane stations restricted if needed.

item.title: Ways to move money in the US: how ACH, bank wire, Zelle and Venmo work
item.description: In the US there are several ways to move money between accounts, and they differ in speed, cost and whether they can be reversed. ACH transfers move in batches, usually in 1–3 business days, cheaply or free, and can be reversed; a bank wire (Fedwire) moves individually, same day, but for a $25–50 fee and with no reversal. Zelle works bank-to-bank in minutes, while Venmo and PayPal hold money in an app balance and move it to your bank over ACH. A reference — facts only.

item.title: Amnesty International: Thailand must not forcibly return two Uyghur men to China
item.description: Two Uyghurs held for more than a decade fear being sent back to China; rights groups warn of a risk of torture and enforced disappearance.

item.title: Houston mayor orders police to limit cooperation with immigration service (ICE)
item.description: John Whitmire: drivers who are stopped but not arrested will no longer be reported to ICE; the decision came after Democrats' election win in Texas.

item.title: Forty Uzbeks to train as chefs to Japanese standards for employment in Japan
item.description: Migration Agency: the programme runs in two stages — six months of Japanese language and cooking in Uzbekistan, then one year of practice in Japan and a state-recognised licence.
